items: On the eighth evening they came braced, for they had been promised a breaking.
The truce was sworn before Zeus himself, father. Lambs and wine and the hands of kings. How does such a thing break?

From above, child. It breaks from above. That is tonight's first terror. The second is a man — a mortal man — who wounds two gods before sundown. And the third... the third is only a husband and wife talking on a wall. You will find it the worst of the three.
Sing, goddess, how the oath was murdered in heaven before it bled on earth.

Two goddesses has Menelaus for helpers — yet there they sit, watching, well pleased... while smiling Aphrodite stands by HER man and plucks him from death. Still — the victory is fair-haired Menelaus's. Come, let us consider: shall we stir evil war again... or make friendship between the peoples? The city of Priam might stand; Menelaus might take Helen home. Peace, perhaps?

Dread son of Cronos — what a word! Would you make VAIN all my labor, the sweat I sweated, my horses worn raw gathering the host against Priam? Do it — and no god will praise you. ...Hear my measure, so you know my hate: three cities are dearest to me in all the world — Argos, Sparta, wide-wayed Mycenae. WASTE THEM, whenever they grow hateful to you; I will not stand before them nor grudge you them — only let Troy die. Send Athena down. Let the TROJANS break the oath first.

Weigh what you have just heard, princes. The queen of heaven has pawned her three best-loved cities of men — populations, cradles, altars — as the price of one city's death. When gods bargain, mortals are the coin. It was ever the exchange rate.
And Athena came down like the star the son of Cronos flings as a sign to sailors or to armies — a blazing thing, shedding sparks — and leapt to the ground between the hosts. And wonder held them all.
...Evil war again, and the screaming?... — ...or friendship between the peoples, from Zeus who deals men war and peace?...

Both armies read the star, and read it both ways. Hold that panel, princes: two hundred thousand men, one portent, and hope and dread in the same breath on every face. Heaven's signs are mirrors. That is why heaven likes them.

And the goddess put on the likeness of a man — Laodocus, Antenor's son — and went hunting through the Trojan ranks for godlike Pandarus, son of Lycaon of the country under Ida: a master archer, a vain heart, and exactly the tool the morning required.

Son of Lycaon — wise heart — dare a thing? Loose one swift arrow at Menelaus... and win glory and gratitude from every Trojan alive, from prince Alexandros FIRST of all. Splendid gifts he would heap on you, surely — if he saw Menelaus, Atreus's warlike son, laid on the sad pyre by YOUR shaft. Come. One arrow. Vow the Wolf-born archer* a hecatomb of firstling lambs, and shoot.
*THE WOLF-BORN ARCHER — Apollo Lykēgenēs, as the Lycians named him: Pandarus's own country-god, whose bow-craft was his boast.

So spoke Athena — and persuaded the fool. Homer's own word for him, princes: the fool. Note what the temptation cost the goddess: nothing true. No bribe was paid, no gift was ever coming, and the glory on offer was the glory of murdering a truce. She simply found the one heart on the field vain enough to hear it as opportunity. Gods do not make men rotten. They shop for the rot that is already there.

And he uncased the famous bow: horn of a wild ibex he had ambushed himself below the crag — sixteen palms the horns — worked, joined, polished, tipped with gold by the horn-wright's craft. The song gives the weapon its whole biography before it lets it shoot. Learn why, princes: so that you understand this arrow was not an accident. It had been being prepared, by vanity and craft and patience, for years. Most treacheries have.
And his good companions ringed him with their shields — lest the Achaeans see and rise before the shot. Mark the shields, princes. Honest arrows need no curtain.

He stripped the lid from the quiver and chose a feathered arrow never shot, freighted with black pains — and vowed his splendid hecatomb to Apollo of the wolf-country — and drew notch and string to his breast, iron to the bow, till the great horn rounded to a circle.
And the bow SANG, and the string CRIED aloud, and the keen shaft leapt — furious to fly through the crowd of men. The truce, princes, is already dead in this panel. It merely has not yet landed.
But the blessed gods did not forget you, Menelaus — the song turns and speaks TO him here, princes, as if the singer himself reached out —

— and first of all the daughter of Zeus stood before you and turned the piercing dart aside — brushed it from your skin AS A MOTHER BRUSHES A FLY FROM HER CHILD LYING SWEETLY ASLEEP — and steered it down where the belt's gold buckles met and the corslet doubled.
Through the wrought belt it drove, through the corslet and the plate beneath, and grazed the man's flesh — and out came the dark blood.

As when a Maeonian or Carian woman stains white ivory with scarlet, to be a cheek-piece for horses — a king's treasure, every horseman's desire — so, Menelaus, were your firm thighs stained with your blood.

And Agamemnon shuddered to see the dark blood run, and Menelaus himself shuddered — and across the whole plain the armies came up off the ground like the sea when the squall lands. The oath of the lambs and the mixed wine, the terms sworn before Zeus and Sun and the powers below — one vain man's arrow, and it is carrion. Remember, princes, that heaven itself procured this. You will need that memory in twenty nights, when heaven begins presenting its invoices about oath-breaking. The gods punish best the crimes they commission.

Dear brother — it was your DEATH I swore with those oaths, setting you alone before Troy!... Yet the oath is not empty, the lambs' blood not wasted: IF the Olympian does not pay it now, he pays it LATE — and men pay him back with interest, with their own heads, their wives, their children. For I know this in my heart: THE DAY WILL COME when holy Ilios perishes, and Priam, and the people of Priam of the good ash spear — Zeus himself will shake the dark aegis over them all, angered for this deceit. — But YOU, Menelaus — if you die, my grief is you: I should sail home in shame to thirsty Argos, the land yearn-worthy, and leave your bones rotting in Trojan earth under an unfinished boast...
Courage — and do not frighten the army yet. The point is not in a fatal place: the wrought belt held it, and the plate beneath. It is a graze with a great noise, brother. Send for a healer.

And Machaon, son of the great healer Asclepius, drew the arrow back through belt and corslet, and sucked the wound, and laid on the gentle salves Chiron once gave his father in kindness. File the healer's face, princes — armies guard such men like water in a desert, and a day comes when an arrow finds HIM, and the whole war turns on his rescue. Meanwhile — look up from the wound. The Trojan ranks are coming on under arms.

Then Agamemnon walked the whole front on foot — and where he found men arming keen, he fed the fire: Idomeneus, steady as a boar; the two Ajaxes with their footmen dense as a storm-cloud a goatherd sees coming over the sea; old Nestor, arraying chariots first, footmen behind, the weak in the middle where they must fight whether they will or no. "Would my knees had your heart's youth, old man," said the king. So far, a good king. Watch what pride does with the next two.
And YOU — master of profitable tricks, cold heart! Why stand you cowering apart, waiting for others to do the dying? First at my feasts, you two — last, it seems, to the fight!

(the dark look) What word has escaped the fence of your teeth, son of Atreus? WE hang back? Stir the war and watch — you will see the father of Telemachus in the FRONT-FIGHTERS of the Trojans' very champions. Your word is wind.
And the king, seeing the anger, smiled and took it all back — he was quick to unsay, our king of kings, which is a virtue that would be greater if he were slower to say.

Quiet, friend. Sit down and hear me. I hold no grudge against Agamemnon, shepherd of the people, for whetting the Achaeans to fight: his will be the glory if we take Troy — and his the great grief if we are cut down. Come — let you and me remember our OWN fury.

Study this exchange like scripture, princes. The king insults him unjustly; he takes it in silence for the office's sake; he silences his own defender; and then he goes and answers with deeds all day. His father's friends called Tydeus a small man who was a great fighter. The son, you are about to learn, is a great fighter who is also a great man. The song is going to give him this entire day. It is called an ARISTEIA* — and his is the pattern of them all.
*ARISTEIA — a hero's day of supreme excellence, when the song pours all its light on one man's fighting.

And as two winter rivers, flooding down the mountains from their great springs, hurl their water together where the ravines meet — and the shepherd hears the thunder far off in the hills — such was the roar and the labor as the armies came together.

Antilochus killed first — Nestor's quick son, first blood of the oath-breaking — and man answered man down the whole line, and the earth began its long drink. The song names them, princes, every one: who, whose son, how, and what home will miss them. I cannot carry every name tonight. But know that the song can, and does, and holds that the naming IS the honoring. No man dies anonymously in Homer. It is the poem's deepest courtesy.

And Ares drove the Trojans, and grey-eyed Athena the Achaeans — and Terror and Rout worked the field, and Strife whose fury never fills, sister of murdering Ares: small at first when she rises, but her head strikes heaven while she walks the earth. The gods you glimpse in the smoke tonight, princes — before this day ends, two of them will bleed.
Forward, Trojans! The best of the Achaeans is hit! — I say he will not bear up long against my bolt — not if the Wolf-lord truly sent me from Lycia!

The archer of the broken truce, at his trade again: Diomedes, through the shoulder, the blood spurting over the corslet — and Pandarus boasting to the whole army. He has perhaps an hour to live, princes. The song lets him spend it exactly like this.

Hear me, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, unwearied one! If ever you stood by my father in the heat of battle — STAND BY ME NOW. Grant me to kill that man — bring him in my spear's cast — who shot me before I saw him and boasts over me that I shall not long see the sun!

Courage, Diomedes: I have put your father's fearless heart in your chest, and TAKEN THE MIST FROM YOUR EYES that till now lay on them — so you shall know a god from a man on this field. Therefore: if a god comes to test you, fight NO immortal — EXCEPT if Aphrodite, daughter of Zeus, comes into the battle. HER you may wound with the sharp bronze.

Enter the strangest license in the whole song, princes: the mist lifted, the sight of gods granted — and one goddess, by name, marked lawful game. Athena has not forgotten a certain apple. Her feuds have a long, exact memory, and today she has found hands for one of them.

And Diomedes went at the Trojans like the river in sudden flood that scatters the dykes — the banks cannot hold it, the vineyard walls cannot check it, when the rain of Zeus drives it — so he stormed the close ranks, and they could not stand though they were many.

Your menace is the son of Tydeus — I know the shield, the helmet-socket, the horses. And I tell you, lord — twice I have hit their best today, Menelaus and this one, TWICE drawn true blood — and only waked them fiercer. My bow was born under a curse. If ever I see home, may a stranger's hand cut my head off if I do not snap this thing across my knee and feed it to the fire — it follows me like wind!

Hear the fool arrive at wisdom one hour late, princes: he blames the BOW. To the last breath, the instrument, never the hand. Come — the song is done with him. Aeneas takes him up into the chariot, and they charge the man with the lifted mist.

Pandarus's last throw pierced the shield and touched the corslet — and he shouted victory with the life already leaving him to say it in. For the spear of Diomedes came back at the shout, and Athena drove it home, and the archer of the broken oath went down in the dust between the armies his one arrow had set back to killing each other. Ledger closed, princes — closed by the very man his second arrow marked. The song's arithmetic is never showy. It is merely exact.

And Aeneas leapt down with shield and long spear and bestrode the body like a lion in its strength — for the Dardanian would not let even a rash ally lie unguarded. Whatever else the years show you of this man, princes, they will never once show you desertion. Remember it in the ash of Issue Eighteen.

Then Tydeus's son took up in one hand a stone — a great deed — a weight not two men could carry, of men such as men are NOW; and he wheeled it and crushed the cup of Aeneas's hip, and the hero went down on his knee with his fist in the earth, and black night began to cover his eyes. And there — but for a mother — the tale of Rome... but no. That is not tonight's song, nor mine to sing.

For his mother had seen. Aphrodite, who bore him to the herdsman Anchises on Ida, poured her pale arms about her dear son and wrapped him in a fold of her bright robe, proof against the flying bronze, and carried him out of the war. And the man with the lifted mist saw exactly who she was — and remembered his license.

And Diomedes went after her through the thick of the fighting, knowing her for a god without strength — none of those goddesses who marshal men's wars — and when he caught her through the great press, he lunged.

The bronze tore the skin above the palm, through the robe the Graces themselves had woven — and out flowed the immortal blood of the goddess: ICHOR, such as runs in the blessed gods, who eat no bread and drink no dark wine, and so are bloodless, and are called deathless. She screamed — and flung down her son — and Phoebus Apollo caught him in his arms in a dark blue cloud, lest some Achaean spear find his life. Two catches in one panel, princes: the god caught the hero, and the war caught a goddess. The second had never happened in the memory of men.

YIELD, daughter of Zeus, from war and fighting! Is it not enough that you ambush the strength of WOMEN? Haunt the war, and I promise you — you will learn to shudder at the word "battle" when you hear it from a distance!

And the goddess of desire fled the field of Troy — bleeding, mocked by a mortal, her wounded wrist cradled — the goddess, princes, for whose verdict on a mountain all these men are dying. The song's irony has no bottom. Do not laugh yet. Her exit is about to be gentler than anything on the field below deserves.
Dear brother — save me! Give me your horses to reach Olympus — I am hurt — A MORTAL wounded me — Tydeus's son, who would fight Father Zeus himself today!

Endure, my child, and bear up, though it grieves you. Many of us who keep Olympus have taken hurt from men... And this Diomedes — the fool does not know the man who fights the gods does not live long; his children do not climb his knee calling "father" when he comes home from war. Let him look to it — lest a better than you meet him some day.

Mark the mother's curse inside the mother's comfort, princes — "his children will not climb his knee." The song will remember that blessing-shaped threat when Diomedes's homecoming is sung. Nothing said on Olympus is ever only said.
Father — will you be angry if I guess? Cyprian went urging some Achaean woman to follow her beloved Trojans... and scratched her slim hand on a golden pin.
Not for you, my child, are the works of war. Attend to the lovely works of MARRIAGE — and leave all this to rushing Ares and Athena.

And the father of gods and men SMILED, and called the golden one to him, and set her right with a sentence. So heaven laughs its daughter whole again — while on the plain her blood-price is still being paid in men. You have seen this joint before, princes, two songs ago, at the feast after the nod. Homer keeps pressing the two worlds together and letting YOU feel the cold. It is the engine of the whole poem. Do not let it become comfortable.

And Apollo made a phantom — an image of Aeneas to the life, in the very armor — and around that empty thing the two armies went on killing one another. There is no colder panel in the song, princes, and no truer one: half the wars of men are fought around eidola. — The true man, meanwhile, lay in Apollo's great shrine on the height, and Leto and Artemis of the arrows healed him and made him more splendid than before.

But Diomedes — Diomedes in his fury charged APOLLO HIMSELF: three times he went in to kill his man, and three times the god turned the bright shield; the license said Aphrodite, princes, and the fury has stopped reading licenses. Watch the fourth charge.
THINK, son of Tydeus — and GIVE WAY. Do not will yourself equal to the gods. NEVER of the same order are the race of deathless gods and the race of men who walk the earth.

And Tydeus's son gave ground — not far, the song says, but back — avoiding the wrath of the Archer. Write the sentence over your lintels, princes; it is the boundary-stone of the whole heroic world, spoken by its coldest surveyor: NOT OF THE SAME ORDER, GODS AND MEN. Tonight one man has bent that law double and lived. No other man in the whole cycle will get his price. Ask Patroclus. Ask, at the gate, Achilles. But those are songs to come.

Hector — where has your courage gone that you had? You boasted once you could hold this city without armies, without allies, alone with your brothers — I look for them today and see NOT ONE: they cower like dogs around a lion. WE do the fighting, we your ALLIES! I have come a long, long way — from whirling Xanthus, from Lycia, where my dear wife is, my infant son, my great estates a poor man dreams of — and even so I drive my Lycians forward and stand my own ground in the front, though nothing of mine is here for a Greek to carry off. And YOU stand — not even ordering your people to hold their wives' walls!

Sarpedon's rebuke, princes — and hear what makes it terrible: every word is fair. He fights for nothing but the oath of allies, farthest from home of any man on the field, and he has earned the right to flay the crown prince in public. Hector says not one word back. He goes through the whole line instead — and the battle turns. Some men answer rebukes. The best men answer FOR them.

And Hector ranged the whole army, and the line came round like a ship answering her steering-oar — and to their joy past believing, AENEAS came back to them alive and whole out of the god's shrine, and they asked him nothing, for the work was too thick for questions. And before the Trojan front went ARES himself, and Hector beside him.

Friends — how we marvel at Hector the spearman, the bold heart! But BESIDE him always walks some god who wards ruin from him — and NOW it is Ares there, in the likeness of a man. Give ground — faces to the Trojans, backs never — and do not rage to fight with gods.

Study the shudder, princes; it is worth the whole aristeia. The one mortal alive with the sight to KNOW a god on the field, and license enough in his blood today to have wounded two — and what he does with that knowledge is RETREAT, in good order, at once. Valor that cannot read a boundary is only expensive noise. Diomedes could read. It is why, of all tonight's heroes, HE gets old.

Then Athena, unseen beneath the cap of Hades, turned the war-god's spear to waste air — and Diomedes drove in his own, and PALLAS ATHENA LEANED ON IT, and it went home in the flank of Ares where the war-belt girded him. And brazen Ares BELLOWED — loud as nine thousand men, as ten thousand cry in battle when they join the strife of war — and trembling took the armies both.

A mortal's spear, a goddess's weight behind it, and the god of war itself screaming over the field he owns. This is the summit of the day the song calls Diomedes's — and mark precisely, princes, WHOSE hands were where. The man supplied the courage and the cast; heaven supplied the license, the sight, the deflection, and the leaning. The heroic bargain in one picture: glory is real, and it is never wholly yours. The wise heroes know it at the time. The others learn it from the fall.
And Ares went up to heaven like the darkness that stands in the sky out of the heat, when the storm-wind rises foul — so brazen Ares showed to Diomedes as he went up huge in cloud to Olympus.

Father Zeus — does it not ANGER you, seeing these violences? Always the gods suffer horrors by each other's wills, doing favors to MEN — and all of us are at war with YOU, for you fathered that mad girl of ruin, Athena! The rest of us obey you — HER you never check with word or deed, you let her run — because you bore the destroyer yourself! Now she has set Tydeus's son raging on the very immortals — Cypris first at the wrist, and then ME —

Do not sit whimpering at my knee, TURNCOAT. Most hateful to me are you of all gods who hold Olympus: forever strife is dear to you, and wars and fighting. You have your mother's unbearable, unbending temper — Hera's, whom I can scarcely rule with words... Yet I will not bear it longer, that you suffer pain. FOR YOU ARE MY SON: to me your mother bore you. But had you been born so ruinous of any other god — long since you would lie lower than the sons of heaven in the pit.

And Paeeon sprinkled the healing simples, and the wound closed as fast as fig-juice curdles white milk when a man stirs it — for the god was in nothing made of dying stuff. And Hebe bathed him and dressed him fresh, and he sat down by Zeus exulting in his glory, learning, as ever, nothing. So ended the day two gods bled: with all wounds closed in heaven, and none closed on earth. And Hera of Argos and Athena of Alalcomenae went home content: they had stopped man-slaughtering Ares from his slaughtering — for one afternoon — by slaughtering. Heaven's accounts, princes. Be glad you keep earthly books.

Then the gods left the field to the men — and the battle swayed, this way, that way, between Simois and the streams of Xanthus, with no radiance in the haze but bronze. And it was now, with heaven gone, that the war showed a face worse than any god's. Watch the king of men, princes. Watch him closely, and remember Aulis.

Take me alive, son of Atreus — take a worthy ransom! Treasures lie thick in my rich father's house — bronze and gold and wrought iron — and my father would give you boundless price to hear I live at the ships of the Achaeans!

And the plea persuaded the heart in Menelaus's breast — Menelaus, princes, the wronged man himself, ten years wronged, softening with his enemy's arms around his knees — and he was on the point of giving him living into his companion's hands —

Soft, Menelaus?! What tenderness is this — did TROJANS deal so gently with YOUR house?! Let NOT ONE of them escape sheer destruction at our hands — NOT the boy his mother still carries in her womb — not even HE — but let all Ilios perish together, unmourned and unmarked!

So he spoke, and turned his brother's heart — urging DOOM, the song says plainly — and Adrestus died at the king's own spear. And old Nestor's cry came down the lines: "kill now, strip the spoils after." I will not gloss this page for you, princes. The song does not. It sets the sentence about the unborn child in the mouth of the king of kings and lets it stand in the record forever — the exact hour the war for an oath became something the oath's gods themselves will one day charge for. The pyres of Issue Eighteen are lit here, on this page, by this speech.

So Helenus read the day: it is Diomedes now who must be prayed away — this new terror they reckoned wilder than Achilles himself. And Hector obeyed his brother the seer. Mark the errand, princes: the best man on the field leaves the field at its worst hour — to organize a PRAYER. Everything Troy is, is in that sentence.

And Hector went through the host and stiffened it to stand — and then he ran for the city, and the dark oxhide rim of the great body-shield tapped at his ankles and his neck as he ran. Homer follows the shield's rhythm the whole way, princes — tap, tap, tap — the sound of one man carrying a city. Learn the detail's trade: it is how the song makes you love a man in one line, so that it can break you with him in three nights' time.
Pray. Pray to the gods, all of you, each in turn. For sorrows are hung over many.

That is all he can give them — the truth, gently, in five words. And the panel is the whole war from the walls' side, princes: a wall of upturned asking faces, and one honest man who will not lie to them and cannot save them. Hold this gate in your mind. Tonight's song ends at this gate, with one particular woman's question.

Who are YOU, magnificent one, of mortal men? Never have I seen you in the fighting before — yet here you stand out in front of everyone in your daring, to wait for my long spear. Doomed are the fathers whose sons face my strength! ...But if you are some IMMORTAL come down from heaven — I have learned today's lesson: I will not fight the gods of heaven. Not I. But if you are a man, who eats the fruit of the field — come on, and enter the nets of death the faster!
Hear the day in his challenge, princes: the man who speared two gods this morning now checks the address before he throws. Wisdom, in the heroic age, is mostly scar tissue in the right places.

Great-hearted son of Tydeus — why ask my lineage? AS THE GENERATION OF LEAVES, SO ARE THE GENERATIONS OF MEN. The leaves — the wind scatters them to the earth, and the living wood breeds others, and spring comes round again: so with men — one generation grows, and another passes away. ...But if you would truly know it, hear then — many men know the tale.

Stop, princes. Whatever else you carry out of this hall in your lives, carry these lines. A young man facing a spear was asked "who are you," and he answered with the truth about everyone. The song will let the two of them walk away friends in a moment — but it has already given you the reason wars are absurd and honor is real in the same four lines. There is no contradiction. There is only the wind, and what men do standing in it.

And Glaucus told his line: Sisyphus's blood; and Bellerophon the blameless, whom a queen's lie exiled with sealed signs of his own death in his hand — who killed the Chimaera, breather of fire; who beat the Solymi and the Amazons and the picked ambush of Lycia to the last man — and won the kingdom and the king's daughter; and whom the gods, late and unexplained, came to hate. Of his blood, Hippolochus; of Hippolochus, "me — and my father sent me to Troy with the words all our fathers say: ALWAYS BE BEST, AND HOLD YOUR HEAD ABOVE OTHERS, AND DO NOT SHAME THE BLOOD." The commission of every heir in this hall, princes. Now watch what the name of the grandfather does to the spear of the enemy.

Then you are my GUEST-FRIEND* from our fathers' fathers, and old! Noble Oeneus my grandsire hosted blameless Bellerophon in his halls twenty days — and they gave each other fine gifts of friendship: Oeneus a war-belt bright with scarlet, Bellerophon a two-handled cup of gold — I left it standing in my house when I came away. So I am your host deep in Argos, and you are mine in Lycia, whenever I come to that country. THEREFORE: let us avoid each other's spears, even in the thick press — Trojans enough for me to kill, whomever a god grants and my feet overtake; Achaeans enough for you to strip, whomever you can. And let us EXCHANGE ARMOR, you and I, so that these all may know we declare ourselves guest-friends from our fathers' time.

*GUEST-FRIEND (xenos) — the hereditary guest-bond, first sworn in this song at a wedding-court two hundred pages ago: it binds the grandsons of the men who swore it, across enemy lines, above the war itself.

And they leapt down and clasped hands and pledged the faith — in the space between two armies, in the middle of the worst day of the war so far. Every man on both sides watched two champions meet at the killing-ground and part as kin. THIS is xenia, princes — the law you learned at Sparta's feast when it was broken. Here it is kept, at full cost, in the fire. The war around these two men is BEING FOUGHT over this law. And the law, for one panel, is stronger than the war. That is the whole moral architecture of the cycle, standing in the open field in plain daylight.

But then — the song cannot resist, and neither can I — Zeus son of Cronos took the wits of Glaucus clean away: for he exchanged with Diomedes GOLD armor for BRONZE — the worth of a hundred oxen for the worth of nine. And with that one dry line, princes, the master does a thing only he dares: he lets the sublime and the ledger stand in one scene and diminish nothing. The bond is holy. The bargain is terrible. Both are true; men are like this; the wind takes all the leaves regardless. Now — through the gate with Hector, for the women are waiting, and the third terror of the night is a small one: a helmet, and a child.

Bring me no wine, honored mother, lest you unstring my knees and I forget my strength. And I dread to pour dark wine to Zeus WITH UNWASHED HANDS — there is no praying to the black-cloud son of Cronos spattered as I am with blood and filth. YOU — take the robe, the loveliest and greatest in the house, the one dearest to yourself, and lay it on the knees of bright-haired Athena in her shrine on the height, and vow twelve yearling heifers if she will pity the town, and the Trojans' wives, and the little children — if she will hold the son of Tydeus back from holy Ilios.

Lady Athena, guardian of the city, shining among goddesses — BREAK the spear of Diomedes — grant that he fall on his face before the Scaean gates — and we will sacrifice twelve yearling heifers in your shrine, if you will pity the town, and the wives of the Trojans, and the little children.

So she prayed. BUT PALLAS ATHENA TURNED HER FACE AWAY. One line, princes — the coldest line in the whole day of cold lines. The women of Troy, who judged no goddess on any mountain, laid their best at the knees of heaven for their children's lives — and heaven, still keeping the account of a beauty contest, refused the robe. When your priests tell you the gods of the old songs are just, tell them you have read the sentence about the robe. And when they tell you the gods are indifferent — tell them you have read the whole rest of the song. Both truths, princes. The old faith carried both without flinching. Carry them.

Strange man. It is not DECENT — this grudge you nurse in your heart while the people die at the wall and the war-cry burns around the city — and the war is YOURS. You would fight any other man yourself whom you saw hanging back from it. Up — before the town is kindled over our heads.

Hector — the rebuke is fair, not more than fair... It was not so much anger at the Trojans that kept me here as grief; I wished to give myself to sorrow a while. But my wife has just now been turning me to the war with her soft words, and I think myself it is better so — victory shifts its men. Wait while I arm — or go, and I will overtake you.

Brother — brother of a scheming, cold-hearted DOG of a woman — would that on the day my mother bore me the storm-wind had carried me to a mountain, or into the wave of the loud sea, and the water taken me before all this was done!... But since the gods ordained these evils so — would I had been the wife at least of a BETTER man, one who felt the world's outrage and its shame. THIS one — his wits are not fast now and will not be after, and I think he will harvest the fruit of it... But come, brother, in and sit; rest your heart a moment — you whom the war-toil rings hardest of all, FOR MY SAKE, dog that I am, and for Alexandros's madness: on whom Zeus has set an evil doom, SO THAT EVEN IN TIME TO COME WE MAY BE SONGS FOR MEN HEREAFTER.

Stop the loom, princes, and look at what she has woven. "That we may be songs for men to come." SHE IS SPEAKING OF US. This hall — this fire — your faces — tonight — WE are the doom Zeus set on her; we are the fruit of her ruin; every night I sing her, I collect a debt she named three thousand nights ago and knew she was paying. No other singer's people ever looked out of the song at the audience like this. Hold still while she looks at you. ...She has gone back to her weaving now. And Hector has not sat down. He never sits down. Come — his wife is waiting at the gate, and I have put it off as long as songs allow.

He went to his own house and did not find her — she was on the wall, weeping, mad with fear for him, the child in the nurse's arms behind her. And at the Scaean gate — the gate you were told to hold in mind — she came running to meet him, Andromache, daughter of great-hearted Eetion... You know the father's name, princes. You watched his mound raised, and the elms planted, two songs ago. Now watch what Thebe's ruin built.

Possessed one — your own strength will destroy you! And you have no pity on your infant son, nor on doomed me, who will soon be your widow: for soon the Achaeans will all rush on you and kill you. And for me, once I lose you, better to go under the earth — there is no other comfort after, only griefs. I HAVE NO FATHER, NO HONORED MOTHER: my father great Achilles killed when he sacked Thebe of the high gates — killed Eetion, yet did not strip him, his heart shamed at that, but burned him in his wrought armor and heaped his mound, and the mountain nymphs planted elms around it. And SEVEN BROTHERS I had in our halls — all of them, in ONE DAY, went down to Hades: all seven great Achilles slew among the shambling cattle and white sheep. And my mother — ransomed, then struck down by Artemis's arrows in her father's house. HECTOR — YOU are my father now, and my honored mother, and my brothers — and you are my strong young husband. Pity us. Stay HERE on the tower. Do not make your child an orphan, your wife a widow.

Every clause of that speech, princes, was purchased in the raid-years — I showed you the receipts. The Iliad's tenderest scene stands on the Iliad's cruelest arithmetic, and the same man's name is on both. The song knows. She knows. SHE IS ASKING TROY'S SHIELD TO HIDE, and she has EARNED the asking, and he must refuse her — and he knows exactly what his refusal costs, better than she does. Now hear her last card — the soldier's card.

— At least then station the ARMY by the fig tree, where the city is easiest climbed and the wall lies open to assault! THREE TIMES their best have come and tried it there — the two Ajaxes, famed Idomeneus, the Atreidae, Tydeus's fierce son — whether some seer told them, or their own hearts drive them to it!

Mark where her hand points, princes, and feel the whole cycle shudder: THE WEAK STRETCH. The seam in the wall. You have known about it since the first song — gods built those walls, and one span of them was mortal work — and now Homer himself sets Troy's best-loved woman pointing straight at it with her child beside her, telling you the enemy's captains ALREADY CIRCLE IT LIKE WASPS. The songs agree with each other across the centuries, princes; that is how you know you are hearing one loom. What enters the city at last, enters THERE. She is pointing at the door of the horse. She is pointing at it to save him.

All this is my care also, wife. But I would stand in terrible shame before the Trojans, and the Trojan women with their trailing robes, if like a coward I skulked apart from the war. Nor does my own heart consent — for I have LEARNED to be brave always, and to fight in the front ranks of the Trojans, winning great glory for my father and myself.

For I know this well in my mind and in my heart: THE DAY WILL COME WHEN HOLY ILIOS WILL PERISH, and Priam, and the people of Priam of the good ash spear. Yet not the Trojans' coming grief moves me so much — not Hecuba's own, not lord Priam's, not my many brave brothers' who will fall in the dust under enemy men — as YOURS: when some bronze-shirted Achaean leads you away weeping, and takes your day of freedom from you; and in Argos you weave at another woman's loom, and carry water from a foreign spring, hating it, and hard necessity on you; and someone says, seeing your tears fall: "THAT WAS HECTOR'S WIFE — the best fighter of the horse-taming Trojans, when they fought around Ilios." And your grief is new again, for the lack of such a man to ward off the day of slavery. BUT LET ME BE DEAD, AND THE HEAPED EARTH HIDE ME, BEFORE I HEAR YOUR CRY AS THEY DRAG YOU AWAY.

There is nothing I can add, princes, and I will not insult the master by trying. Only this: he has just told her the city dies, she is enslaved, and he cannot save her — and every future clause of it is TRUE, and both of them almost know it — and in the next breath, watch: the whole scene turns on a baby frightened by a hat. That turn — grief to laughter in one reach of the arms — no singer has matched it since, and none will. Attend.

So speaking, shining Hector reached for his son — and the child shrank back screaming against the nurse's breast, terrified at the sight of his own father: frightened by the bronze, and the horsehair crest he saw nodding dreadful from the helmet's top.

And his dear father laughed aloud, and his honored mother — LAUGHED, princes, both of them, on the wall of the dying city, between the prophecy and the fact — and Hector took the helmet from his head and laid it all-shining on the ground. And he kissed his dear son and swung him in his arms.

Zeus and you other gods — grant that this my child become, as I am, preeminent among Trojans, as strong and brave; and rule Ilios in his strength. And let a man say of him one day, "HE IS FAR BETTER THAN HIS FATHER," as he comes home from war bearing the bloody spoils of the enemy he killed — AND LET HIS MOTHER'S HEART REJOICE.

Hear the shape of the hope, princes: not "let him live" — the age did not insult its sons with safety — but "let him outshine me, and let her be there, glad." Hold the prayer against everything you know is coming, and understand at last why the ledger made you memorize a baby's name three songs ago. I will say no more. The song forbids it here.

And she went home turning back again and again, letting the big tears fall, and in Hector's own house the serving-women raised the death-wail FOR HIM STILL LIVING — for none of them believed he would come home again from the Achaeans' hands. And Paris overtook him at the gate, glittering like the stallion that snaps his rope and gallops ringing to the river — and Hector had not the heart to be hard with him any longer, for the man had come. And the two sons of Priam went out of the gate together, toward the noise. So ends the sixth book of the master's song, princes — on a wife who mourns the living, a child who fears the crest, a laugh, a prayer, and a door. Every war that ever was, is on that wall. That is why the wall still stands, in the singing, when every stone of it is three thousand years down.
You warned us, father. The husband and wife on the wall — worse than the arrow, worse than the bleeding gods. Why is it WORSE?

Because the gods healed, child. Ichor closes like milk curdling; Ares sat down whole beside his father by supper. But there is no Paeeon for the wall-scene — no simple that closes "let me be dead before I hear your cry." The gods' wounds tonight were spectacle. The mortals' wound was a PROMISE. And you have eighteen more nights of watching it kept.
And she told him where the wall is weak, princes. To save him. Remember — when the time comes — that the door of Troy's death was first pointed out in love.
Enough. The truce is carrion; Pandarus is paid; two gods have bled and learned nothing; a king has cursed the unborn; a goddess has refused a robe; and Hector has gone back out through the gate.

Tomorrow Hector duels the tower of the army and the two part exchanging GIFTS — this war still remembers, sometimes, what men owe each other. Then a wall rises in a night, an embassy walks a beach in the dark to a proud man's fire... and the proudest sentence in the whole song is spoken over a heap of treasure. Sleep, child. Tomorrow the wrath is offered everything — and refuses.

"As the generation of leaves, so are the generations of men: the wind scatters the leaves upon the earth, and the living wood breeds others when spring comes again; so one generation of men grows, and another passes away."
— after the words of Glaucus the Lycian to Diomedes, spoken between the armies.
